case_for.text: FY2025 converted USD 58.7bn of revenue into USD 48.1bn of gross profit and USD 13.7bn of operating income, the strongest operating margin the record holds. This leg is evidenced in the only sense that matters for a starting point: it is disclosed, not forecast, and carrying the latest year's operating margin across every forecast year is what the figure beside this case reflects. The single observation that would falsify it is a reported period showing operating margin below the latest year's level with no one-off cause disclosed alongside it.
case_for.lead_in: The margin leg is reported, not assumed

case_for.text: Revenue has compounded at 9.05% on the recorded ten-year measure, and it is that compound pace rather than the slower latest year that the discounted cash flow's forecast path carries forward off the FY2025 base — the forecast is a continuation case, and should be read as one. The bull leg asks for more than continuation: growth at the record's fastest annual pace in every forecast year, which is the value printed beside this case. It is falsified by two consecutive reported periods of revenue growth below the latest year's rate.
case_for.lead_in: The decade compounds faster than the latest year

case_for.text: Measured on monthly observations, the equity's beta of 0.277 produces a cost of equity of 6.46% — a defensive hurdle that lifts the present value of cash flows far out in the forecast and makes the terminal assumption unusually forgiving. Our judgement is that this is the quietest support under the valuation and the least discussed: it rests on a historical regression against the index, not on a forward view of risk. A single re-measurement over a period including a policy shock would raise beta and undo much of it.
case_for.lead_in: A low hurdle rate does the terminal work

case_against.text: The Form 20-F dated February 2026 incorporates the therapy area and business review material by reference rather than setting it out, so the size, market and timing of the exclusivity step-down — and what sits just beyond the twelve-month horizon — are not in the evidence before us; that leg of the thesis is unevidenced and cannot be scored either way. What is disclosed is the cost of defending against it: FY2025 research and development of USD 14.2bn. Run revenue growth at its slowest recorded rate throughout the forecast, as the bear leg requires, and the printed value shows what a step-down is worth. It is falsified by a product-level exclusivity schedule placing the material losses beyond the horizon.
case_against.lead_in: The exclusivity step-down is unevidenced here

case_against.text: Anyone arguing that growth slows must accept that the valuation on the same record does not: its forecast path compounds off the FY2025 base at the ten-year pace of 9.05%, faster than the latest year grew, so a deceleration view is an argument against that valuation rather than support for it. Held at the latest year's growth rate in every forecast year, the value per share falls, as printed beside this case. The leg is falsified by a reported year in which revenue growth exceeds the recorded ten-year compound rate.
case_against.lead_in: Deceleration and the forecast cannot both hold

case_against.text: No document before us sets out the US pricing policy or any quantified price effect, so the direction of margin under it is unevidenced and asserted by neither case on this record. Comparability of the margin history is itself qualified: effective 1 January 2025 the group updated its presentation of gross margin, having previously cited a different metric. Strike the operating margin at its lowest recorded level and the printed value shows what sustained price compression costs; the leg is falsified by margin holding at the latest year's level through the next reported periods with pricing terms disclosed alongside.
case_against.lead_in: Margin direction under US pricing policy is unevidenced

content.the_question: Both cases read the same record: FY2025 revenue of USD 58.7bn, gross profit of USD 48.1bn, operating income of USD 13.7bn, and revenue compounding at 9.05% on the recorded ten-year measure. They differ on whether that record is the base rate for the years ahead, or the high-water mark before an exclusivity step-down and US pricing policy bend growth and margin down — and the evidence in front of us documents the record while saying nothing about either forward driver.

content.commentary: AstraZeneca is a biopharmaceutical company that discovers, develops, manufactures and commercializes prescription medicines, generating revenue primarily from product sales to healthcare systems, physicians, pharmacies and patients across multiple therapy areas. Its 20-F disclosures state that the group's Science and Executive Team reviews performance on an integrated basis for the business as a whole, substantially in the form of the group's IFRS financial statements, rather than tracking the profitability of individual drugs or drug classes; this reflects an industry economics where the high upfront cost of discovering and developing new medicines, paired with comparatively low and stable unit production costs, breaks the direct link between an individual product's revenue and its associated margin seen in many manufacturing businesses. Consistent with this, capital expenditure, in-licensing and R&D resources are allocated across the group on a needs and merit basis under Early-Stage and Late-Stage Product Committees rather than against discrete product-level budgets. For fiscal year 2025 the group reported total revenue of approximately 58.7 billion US dollars, with cost of revenue of approximately 10.6 billion US dollars leaving gross profit of approximately 48.1 billion US dollars, an implied gross margin consistent with a research-intensive pharmaceutical business where manufacturing cost is a small share of the sales price. In the second quarter of 2025 alone the group generated revenue of approximately 14.5 billion US dollars and gross profit of approximately 12.0 billion US dollars. Operating income for fiscal year 2025 was approximately 13.7 billion US dollars, after research and development spending of approximately 14.2 billion US dollars and selling, general and administrative expense of approximately 19.9 billion US dollars for the year, underscoring the scale of investment the company directs toward its innovation pipeline and commercial infrastructure relative to reported revenue. The evidence available for this note does not include a therapy-area or brand-level revenue split, nor a geographic breakdown of sales or manufacturing sites, so no segment-level revenue mix or operating footprint detail can be stated with support here; readers should treat the business as reporting on an integrated, group-wide basis rather than through disclosed product or regional segments for the purposes of this overview. What can be said with confidence is that the company operates as a single, internally managed pharmaceutical enterprise whose revenue is earned through the sale of prescription medicines, with resource allocation and performance review conducted at the group level rather than product-by-product.

AstraZeneca's fiscal year 2025 revenue of $58.74 billion breaks out only by geography in the disclosures reviewed for this note; product-level and therapy-area revenue splits, and the FY2024 comparative figures needed to gauge segment growth, are not present, so growth rates by product or therapy area cannot be stated here. The geographic pattern available shows the United States as the largest single market at $23.97 billion, followed by Europe excluding the United Kingdom at $13.46 billion and the United Kingdom itself at $4.36 billion; these lines are not summed into a combined Europe figure since only the underlying components are on record. Asia, Africa and Australasia together contributed $13.37 billion, within which China alone accounted for $6.64 billion and Japan $3.56 billion; the remainder of that region, and the smaller American markets outside the US, are reported only in grouped lines that are left unallocated rather than apportioned. Group cost of revenue was $10.63 billion against gross profit of $48.11 billion, though margin by segment cannot be derived without a cost split by geography or product, neither of which is present in the material reviewed. Segment-level capital expenditure and a like-for-like revenue history are likewise absent, so no view on relative reinvestment or run-rate momentum by segment can be given here. On exclusivity, the intended approach was to inventory dated loss-of-exclusivity events per molecule and market through 2029, tagging each as a revenue step inside the twelve-month view, a plausible anticipation effect beyond it, or undated. The cut-off applied is straightforward: an event dated on or before 31 December 2029 would sit inside the horizon; a later event close enough to be reasonably priced into the current twelve-month view would count as an anticipation effect; anything else falls to the third bucket. In practice, no dated exclusivity or patent-expiry entries — from a US register, an ex-US register, or the 20-F's own expiry table — are present in the material available for this note. Every molecule-market pair that might otherwise be inventoried therefore falls to the undated category, and no expiry-driven view of the revenue base can be offered. This is a material gap for a franchise whose durability depends heavily on patent and regulatory exclusivity, and it should be read as an absence of coverage rather than an assessment that no exposure exists.

content.commentary: AstraZeneca operates within a global oncology-and-specialty-weighted pharmaceutical industry now defined by tightening payer economics rather than by patent expiry alone. Company risk disclosures point to three concurrent policy pressures: the US Inflation Reduction Act, the EU's Joint Clinical Assessment regime, and what the company terms 'health equalisation initiatives' pushing some governments to raise drug spending to share R&D costs more evenly across markets. Beyond this general framing, the evidence available for this note does not contain the CMS Medicare Drug Price Negotiation selected-drug lists, published maximum fair prices, Part D redesign detail, Medicaid rebate or 340B ceiling-price mechanics, any most-favoured-nation or tariff executive action, or China volume-based procurement and reimbursement-list rulings — so no AstraZeneca molecule can be confirmed here as appearing on a published negotiated-price list, and no competitor generic or biosimilar approval status can be verified against those lists. That gap should be read as a limit on this note's specificity, not as evidence of favourable or unfavourable pricing treatment. What the record does support is that AstraZeneca frames commercial risk broadly around price-control measures, patient access, diagnosis rates, IP erosion, prescribing-habit shifts and manufacturing execution, alongside the structural difficulty of operating across politically and economically volatile emerging markets, including counterfeiting and enforcement risk. Industry growth in at least one recent quarter was described by the company as reflecting patient-demand growth and geographic expansion, with quarter-to-quarter variation partly a function of order timing in tender-based markets — a dynamic characteristic of oncology and vaccine procurement in ex-US, non-negotiated markets rather than of US list pricing specifically.

Emerging 'health equalisation' policy discussion pushing some governments to increase drug spending to share R&D costs
Continued reliance on tender-based procurement in several ex-US markets, creating quarter-to-quarter order-timing volatility
Ongoing generic and biosimilar competitive pressure across the industry as a structural risk to branded portfolios
content.competitive_position: AstraZeneca's position rests on scale and an oncology-and-biologics-weighted portfolio that overlaps most directly with Merck, Bristol Myers Squibb and Novartis, and on cardiometabolic exposure shared with Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk; GSK and Sanofi compete more on vaccines and immunology, and Pfizer on broad primary-care and specialty scale with a heavier US weighting. Against these peers AstraZeneca is more exposed to tender-driven and ex-US procurement dynamics than to the US negotiated-price environment specifically, on the evidence available, while carrying the same generic industry-wide risks from IP erosion, biosimilar entry and payer cost-containment that its named comparators face. The durability of this position cannot be assessed against specific negotiated-price or biosimilar-entry data here, since none was available; it instead rests on pipeline execution and geographic diversification, both flagged by the company itself as sources of downside risk if commercial launches, manufacturing or regulatory approval falter.

content.commentary: Evidence available for this section is limited. The 2025 Form 20-F incorporates by reference the extensive governance disclosures normally found in AstraZeneca's Annual Report — including the Chair's Statement, Chief Executive Officer's Review, and the Corporate Governance Report covering board composition, remuneration policy and compliance with the UK Corporate Governance Code — but the specific text of those sections, including named directors, tenure, individual pay awards, and incentive plan structures, was not present in the material available for this note. Consequently we cannot characterise management's track record, board composition, or the mechanics of executive incentive alignment with any specificity here. What can be said is that AstraZeneca continues to file governance and remuneration disclosure through the standard UK annual reporting cycle (20-F incorporating the Annual Report, plus AGM results and interim/final results announcements), consistent with a large-cap UK-listed pharmaceutical issuer subject to the UK Corporate Governance Code's provisions on risk oversight, board committees, and pay-for-performance structures. One disclosed operational note from the reporting period references pressure from generic competition in China and stock compensation effects ahead of anticipated volume-based procurement implementation in China in the first quarter of 2026 — a factor management will need to navigate operationally, though the evidence here does not extend to how leadership is specifically responding or how this is reflected in incentive design. Given the gap in underlying detail, our confidence in any assessment of management quality or governance robustness for this note is low, and we would caution readers against drawing conclusions about compensation appropriateness or governance strength from what is available. We recommend treating this section as provisional pending fuller access to the Corporate Governance Report and Directors' Remuneration Report content.

content.commentary:
Reported annual history on record for AstraZeneca extends to the financial year ended December 2025; the two preceding financial years and the first-half 2026 interim statement are not available here, so what follows reads the structure of the most recent full year rather than a multi-year margin path. Margin ratios are not held as recorded calculations, so the relationships below are given as reported (IFRS) levels. The company's non-IFRS core measures, which exclude items such as intangible amortisation and impairment, are not represented among the figures available, and no reconciliation between core and reported bases can be shown from this record. Any pricing-policy effect on profitability would have to be judged against a margin trend line that the available history does not yet supply.

On a reported basis for FY2025, revenue was USD 58,739m against cost of revenue of USD 10,633m, leaving gross profit of USD 48,106m. Gross profit accordingly represents the great majority of revenue, the profile expected of a branded, patent-protected portfolio. The distance between gross profit and operating profit is set by the operating cost base rather than by cost of goods: SG&A of USD 19,933m was the largest single cost line of the year, ahead of both research and development at USD 14,232m and cost of revenue, and reported operating profit was USD 13,743m. On these levels, reported operating margin is governed far more by commercial and research intensity than by manufacturing economics, and a change in realised price would pass through gross profit almost undiluted before meeting a largely fixed cost base.

Below operating profit, interest expense of USD 1,694m was only partly offset by interest income of USD 360m. Pre-tax income was USD 12,402m and the tax charge USD 2,169m, a low effective burden relative to pre-tax profit, giving net income of USD 10,225m. Reported basic earnings per share were USD 6.60 and diluted earnings per share USD 6.54, so dilution was slight.

One reported-basis feature matters directly for margin comparison. Income from disposals of assets and businesses, where the Group retains no significant ongoing economic interest, is recorded within other operating income and expense, a line that sits above operating profit. Reported operating margin can therefore move with disposal activity independently of underlying trading, which is among the principal reasons core and reported measures diverge in any given year.

The balance sheet at the FY2025 year end shows total assets of USD 114,074m, of which intangible assets were USD 37,846m and goodwill USD 21,242m. The company states that its statement of financial position contains significant investments in intangible assets, including goodwill, and that realising value on them depends on regulatory approvals, market acceptance, competition and legal developments; amortisation and impairment of those balances are precisely the charges core measures adjust away. Cash and equivalents stood at USD 5,711m, with current assets of USD 28,723m against current liabilities of USD 30,617m, a negative working-capital position consistent with funding through payables and short-term borrowing. Reported results are also translation-sensitive: the company reports in US dollars while key product sales and cost currencies include the euro, Chinese renminbi, pound sterling, Japanese yen and Swedish krona, so year-on-year margin comparison carries an exchange component. The company separately flags that unfavourable resolution of product liability claims could require significant provisions. Against this single-year structure, the recorded ten-year compound annual growth rate of 9.05% is the only long-run growth reference available.

red_flags: Impairment reviews and useful economic lives of intangible assets are company-identified key judgements; reported profit is sensitive to both, and neither is visible in the cash statement.
Litigation provisioning depends on management's assessment of when an adverse outcome becomes probable, a timing judgement the company flags as significant.
Cash taxes paid and prior-year comparatives are not among the available figures, so the accrual gap cannot be checked against cash tax or tracked as a trend.
content.commentary:
Cash conversion for the year to 31 December 2025 was strong and the accrual gap points the right way. Operating cash flow of $14,575 million exceeded reported net income of $10,225 million, so profit was more than covered by cash from operations rather than being carried by accruals.

Part of that spread is ordinary non-cash charge. Share-based compensation of $719 million is added back in the cash statement but remains a real cost to shareholders. Working capital moved little: the recorded change was negative $386.6 million, immaterial against revenue of $58,739 million, so there is no sign that receivables or inventory were stretched to manufacture reported cash.

Capital intensity is modest relative to the cash generated: capital expenditure of $2,810 million absorbed a minority of operating cash flow, leaving cash after investment clearly positive in direction. Research and development of $14,232 million runs through the income statement, and the company identifies the expensing of internal development expenses as a key judgement. Expensing rather than capitalising leaves less room for earnings to be flattered by deferral, though where the line falls is itself an estimate.

Tax and interest are visible but not fully testable. Income tax expense of $2,169 million was recorded against pre-tax income of $12,402 million, alongside interest expense of $1,694 million; cash taxes paid are not among the available figures, so the book-versus-cash tax gap cannot be examined here.

Distributions were funded from operations rather than from borrowing. Dividends paid of $4,971 million were the only cash return to shareholders, with no share repurchase outflow recorded for the period, while debt repayments of $2,029 million far exceeded new debt proceeds of $15 million, within a net financing outflow of $7,544 million. That pattern is consistent with genuine cash generation rather than distributions supported by leverage.

The main quality risks sit in estimates rather than in cash. The company lists revenue recognition, impairment reviews and useful economic lives of intangible assets, business combinations and goodwill, litigation liabilities and taxation among its key judgements and significant estimates. For an acquisitive pharmaceutical group, the timing of intangible impairment and the amortisation life assigned to acquired products are the levers with the largest effect on reported profit, and neither is observable from the cash statement. Legal provisions are recognised only when an adverse outcome is judged probable and reliably estimable, and management describes determining when that threshold is crossed as a key judgement in its own right.

AstraZeneca's balance sheet is asset-heavy and intangible-led rather than cash-rich, and the two dated snapshots available here — the June half-year stage and the December year-end — show liquidity thinning while near-term debt was taken down.

Cash and cash equivalents fell to $5,711m at the December year-end from $7,058m at the half-year stage, with short-term investments immaterial at either date ($30m against $50m). Total current assets were broadly flat at $28,723m versus $28,939m, but the mix shifted away from cash: receivables rose to $15,177m from $14,168m and inventory to $6,557m from $6,467m. Against current liabilities of $30,617m, the group therefore ran a working capital deficit at the year-end — a normal posture for a large-cap pharmaceutical with dependable operating cash generation, but one that leaves the balance-sheet cushion itself slim and places the liquidity runway on operating inflows and undrawn facilities rather than on the cash line.

On leverage, short-term debt roughly halved to $3,104m at the year-end from $6,492m at the half-year stage, consistent with repayment or terming-out of near-dated maturities; long-term debt stood at $24,715m. Average gross debt used for cost-of-capital work is $29,958.5m, carrying a pre-tax cost of debt of 5.65%. Total assets of $114,074m against that debt stack implies modest gross leverage for the sector, though the figures here do not include a reported net debt measure. Management defines net debt as interest-bearing loans and borrowings plus lease liabilities, net of cash, other investments and net derivatives, and flags it explicitly as a non-GAAP measure that cannot be derived directly from the condensed consolidated statements.

Maturity structure is investment-grade and staggered across currencies: the disclosed bond stack comprises callable euro issues designated in cash flow and fair value hedges, a sterling non-callable note and euro paper designated in a net investment hedge, with fixed-rate publicly traded debt marked at year-end quoted prices under Level 1 inputs. Dollar funding has been raised through AstraZeneca Finance notes documented in filings furnished in February 2024, March 2023 and May 2021. One structural point deserves note: the parent services its debt and guarantee obligations out of dividends, distributions and loans from subsidiaries and branches, so creditor access to cash flow runs through the operating entities.

No covenant thresholds, facility sizes or a maturity-by-year schedule are captured in the figures available here, and there is no balance-sheet snapshot later than the December year-end, so the assessment is a year-end one.
observations: Cash fell over the second half while receivables and inventory rose, so the liquid share of an otherwise flat current asset base thinned.
Near-term debt was roughly halved between the half-year and year-end dates, leaving the bulk of borrowings in long-dated form.
Current liabilities exceeded current assets at the year-end; the runway rests on operating cash generation rather than on balance-sheet cash.
Net debt is a company-defined non-GAAP measure and is not derivable from the condensed statements; no covenant or facility detail is available here.

content.commentary:
Cash generation in the year to December 2025 begins with an unusually wide gross margin: revenue of $58,739m produced gross profit of $48,106m, against which selling, general and administrative costs of $19,933m were the largest operating charge. Net cash from operating activities was $14,575m. The distance between gross profit and operating cash is where the work of the business sits — research, commercial spend, tax and working capital all fall between the two lines — so headline margin overstates the rate at which this franchise turns sales into spendable cash.

The uses of that cash are concentrated and predictable. Investing activities absorbed $6,808m, of which capital expenditure was $2,810m; the balance runs through intangibles, business development and financial-asset flows. The annual report shows that the investing line is broader than plant and equipment alone: the replacement share awards issued on the Alexion acquisition are classified within investing, as are the cash flows arising from the monetisation of participation rights linked to the former Synagis arrangement. Financing activities absorbed $7,544m, dominated by dividends of $4,971m and debt repayments of $2,029m against negligible new drawings of $15m. Operating cash flow accordingly covered capital expenditure and the dividend with room left to service and reduce borrowings rather than to fund them.

Classification detail matters when judging durability. Share-based payment expense of $719m is a non-cash charge added back within operating cash flow, but the stated policy places purchases of shares by employee benefit trusts within financing, while employer and employee taxes paid on vesting are recognised in operating activities. The economic cost of equity compensation is therefore split across two sections of the statement rather than sitting wholly against operating cash.

The intra-year shape is informative. In the half-year to June 2025 operating cash flow was $7,099m, with the remainder of the year's generation arriving later; dividends of $3,357m and investing outflows of $3,361m were markedly front-loaded, while financing outflows of $2,189m and capital expenditure of $1,088m were lighter than an even run-rate would imply. Generation is spread more evenly across the year than distributions are, which means interim liquidity, not annual coverage, is the tighter constraint.

One inconsistency in the record is worth flagging. Share repurchases of $489m appear in the first half of 2025, while the full-year repurchase line stands at $0 on a basis dated from January 2013; the annual buyback figure should not be read as a statement that no shares were bought. On working capital, the movement carried in the cash-based valuation work is an outflow of -$387m, modest against operating cash flow of this size, and nothing available indicates a release or absorption large enough to reshape the cash picture. No separate free cash flow measure is on record for the period, and the evidence here does not break operating cash flow into its working capital, tax and interest components; restructuring activity under the post-Alexion programme and the ERP upgrade continues to run through operating and investing lines without a separately quantified cash figure available here.

content.commentary: AstraZeneca's cash flow statement for full-year 2025 shows a company generating substantial operating cash while continuing to invest heavily and return cash to shareholders. Operating cash flow reached $14.6 billion for the year, funding a broad program of investment and distribution. Investing activities absorbed $6.8 billion, consistent with continued capital expenditure of $2.8 billion on manufacturing capacity, R&D infrastructure and other long-lived assets, alongside other investment outflows not itemised here. Financing activities used $7.5 billion, reflecting dividend payments, debt service and other financing flows. Dividends paid over the year totalled roughly $5.0 billion, underscoring management's continued prioritisation of shareholder distributions as a core use of capital, with the company separately declaring a second interim dividend for the year that lifted the total dividend declared for 2025 above the prior year, per the company's own results announcement. On the debt side, the company drew only $15 million in new debt proceeds against $2.0 billion of repayments, indicating net deleveraging activity for the year rather than debt-funded expansion. Share-based compensation of $719 million continued to represent a modest but recurring non-cash charge tied to employee retention and incentive programs. No share repurchases were recorded against the cumulative buyback figure disclosed for the year, suggesting that, on this measure, the company did not return capital via open-market repurchases during the period, in contrast to the modest repurchase activity seen in the first half of the year on a different reporting basis. Diluted shares outstanding stood at approximately 1.562 billion, a figure relevant to per-share metrics investors use to judge the efficiency of capital returned. Overall, the pattern is one of a cash-generative business directing the bulk of its distributable cash toward dividends and reinvestment in the business rather than buybacks, with debt reduction taking priority over new borrowing during the year. The evidence available does not extend to management's stated capital allocation priorities or forward buyback authorisations, so no view is offered on future intentions.

commentary.text: AstraZeneca enters the forward period from an FY2025 revenue base of USD 58.7bn, gross profit of USD 48.1bn and operating income of USD 13.7bn. Quarterly detail on this record is limited to the June 2025 quarter, when revenue was USD 14.5bn.

Management, in results published in February 2026, described growth as driven by continued patient demand and geographic expansion, and noted that third- and fourth-quarter growth rates reflect order timing in certain tender markets. We record this as the company's own characterisation, not as a forecast adopted here. It identifies volume and geography rather than any single product as the reported engine, and it flags tender phasing as quarterly noise that should not be read as trend.

Research and development absorbed USD 14.2bn in FY2025 and USD 3.5bn in the June 2025 quarter, and that spending is the principal claim on future growth. This record carries no dated late-stage readouts or regulatory action dates, so growth is not attributed to named assets or scheduled catalysts here; the company itself states that realising value from its intangible asset base depends on regulatory approvals, market acceptance, competition and legal developments.

Our base case is continued compounding broadly in line with the recorded ten-year revenue CAGR of 9.05%, not a step down from it. We state this explicitly because a deceleration narrative would contradict the discounted values carried elsewhere in this note, which rest on a forward revenue path no slower than that historical rate. A reader who expects maturing franchises to slow the top line should read those enterprise values as correspondingly generous; the two views cannot be held together.

Two base-case enterprise values are recorded: USD 293.7bn on an exit multiple and USD 481.8bn on a Gordon growth terminal. The gap between them is not a measure of pipeline durability and should not be read as one. It follows from two mutually inconsistent terminal conventions applied to the same forecast, the exit-multiple version embedding a far slower — plausibly negative — perpetuity than the growth formulation. With cost of equity recorded at 6.46%, the discount rate is low, so the terminal convention rather than the explicit forecast years dominates either figure.

content.commentary:
The two terminal treatments do not converge, and that is the first thing to take from the exhibit. On the same explicit-period cash flows and the same discount rate, the exit-multiple case puts enterprise value at approximately USD 293.7 billion and the Gordon growth case at approximately USD 481.8 billion; equity value on the exit-multiple case is approximately USD 269.8 billion. The two value-per-share outputs sit correspondingly far apart. This is not a conservative anchor beside an aggressive one. It is a spread wide enough that the exhibit does not discriminate between outcomes: whether these figures imply a re-rating at all depends entirely on which terminal convention the reader accepts, and the distance between the two methods, set out above, is better read as the headline result than as a footnote to it.

The gap follows from two mutually inconsistent conventions rather than from anything about the business. An exit multiple fixes terminal value against terminal-year earnings and leaves the perpetual growth it implies to fall out of the arithmetic; a Gordon growth terminal value fixes growth and lets the multiple fall out. Comparing the perpetual growth the exit multiple implies with the terminal growth assumption used in the other case explains the spread on its own terms. Attributing that spread to the durability of the product portfolio would dress a modelling artefact as a finding; nothing in this exhibit measures durability. The terminal value share of each case, also set out above, indicates how little of either result the explicit forecast window carries.

The discount rate is the other lever, and it is a soft one. Cost of equity of 6.46% rests on a beta of 0.277; with debt weighted at 10.4% of capital at market value and an after-tax cost of debt of 4.52% against a pre-tax 5.65%, the WACC sits close to the cost of equity. A beta at that level is doing a great deal of work. In our judgement a higher beta would compress both cases, and the Gordon growth case by more, because a perpetuity value turns on the narrow spread between WACC and terminal growth — the very quantity a low rate makes small. The width of the result range is thus in large part a property of a low discount rate meeting a perpetuity formula.

The cash generation underneath is the sturdier part of the picture. FY2025 operating cash flow of USD 14,575 million against capital expenditure of USD 2,810 million leaves a substantial free cash base, and a working capital change of negative USD 386.6 million is immaterial beside it, so working capital intensity is not a swing factor here. Revenue of USD 58,739 million and operating income of USD 13,743 million anchor the EBIT margin assumption. Compound revenue growth of 9.05% over ten years is the reference point for judging the revenue growth assumption: a full-cycle rate rather than a run rate, and not one to extend casually.

What a consolidated model of this kind cannot see is visible in the company's own valuation work. Its 20-F for the year ended 31 December 2025 describes impairment testing that values product, marketing and distribution rights using discounted cash flows risk-adjusted for the probability of technical and regulatory success, peak year sales and sales erosion following patent expiry, with net impairment charges recognised in that year. A consolidated model has no equivalent machinery: patent expiry shape and pipeline attrition reach it only through the revenue growth, margin and terminal assumptions.

Both outputs are model results conditional on the named assumptions above — beta, cost of equity, WACC, terminal growth, the exit multiple, revenue growth, EBIT margin and the intensity assumptions — and neither is a price target. The defensible conclusion is narrow: the cash base supports a substantial enterprise value, and the choice of terminal convention, not the operating record, determines which number one ends up holding.

Two base-case enterprise values sit on the record, built on the same near-term cash flows and differing only in how the horizon is closed: USD 293.7bn on an exit multiple, USD 481.8bn on a Gordon growth perpetuity. That distance measures the disagreement between two terminal conventions, not pipeline durability or franchise quality; nothing on record reconciles the two treatments. No bear or bull enterprise value exists, so the cases below vary assumptions in words and attach no value to them.

FY2025 revenue of USD 58.7bn is the base; the recorded ten-year compound growth rate is 9.05%. We assume deceleration below that pace as larger molecules approach loss of exclusivity "" a judgement, not a recorded forecast. This assumption and the revenue path embedded in the enterprise values above are not demonstrably the same path; if that path compounds at or above the historical rate, both enterprise values should be read as upper bounds on our assumption set rather than as its output. Full-year results attribute growth to patient demand and geographic expansion, with quarterly rates reflecting tender order timing.

Erosion deeper and earlier on molecules losing exclusivity inside the horizon, a US price haircut on molecules named for CMS negotiation, and a failed oncology readout. Which molecules expire when, and which are listed, is not set out in the record available here, so depth and timing are parameters we vary rather than source. The pricing environment supports the direction: the 20-F cites payer measures to limit healthcare spending and tariff or trade action that raises costs or reduces revenues, and Q4 2025 carried an unfavourable gross-to-net adjustment.

Double-digit volume growth with expanded class leadership, as reported for the period, persists across the horizon; erosion is shallower and later; the dated readouts convert into launches. Only in this case is the Gordon growth figure something other than arithmetic.

Expiries falling just past the explicit forecast window change no in-horizon revenue yet can compress the multiple well before they land. content.sensitivity_commentary: Discount rate and terminal assumption move this valuation more than any operating variable. The recorded beta of 0.277, from monthly observations, gives a cost of equity of 6.46%; with a debt weight of 10.4%, a cost of debt of 5.65% and an after-tax cost of debt of 4.52%, the blended rate is low for a business whose outcomes are binary "" trials read out or they do not, patents hold or they do not. A fifth-year discount factor of 0.738 penalises distant cash flows lightly. Directionally, a beta capturing more of those binary events raises the cost of equity and reduces both values, hitting the Gordon growth case hardest because most of its value sits past the explicit horizon; a lower terminal growth rate works the same way.
